extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of philosophy interested in mysticism, epistemology, and the relation of intuition and reason
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing mysticism and mystical metaphysics — i.e., how to judge claims that rest on intuition/insight (vs. analytic reason), unity/monism, the unreality of time, and the ontological status of good and evil. Focuses on appropriate tests, limits, and proper role of intuition and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insight (intuition) must be tested and supported
rubrics_metrics.description: "Insight, untested and unsupported, is an insufficient guarantee of truth, in spite of the fact that much of the most important truth is first suggested by its means."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat intuition as a source of hypotheses or suggestions rather than as final proof. Subject intuitive convictions to further examination, comparison with other beliefs, and where possible to empirical or logical tests. Be wary of relying on subjective conviction alone; seek corroboration by reason and mutual compatibility of beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and compare reason and intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Question I posed: "Are there two ways of knowing, which may be called respectively reason and intuition? And if so, is either to be preferred to the other?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly evaluate whether a claimed 'way of knowledge' is intuition/revelation or discursive reason. Assess relative applicability and trustworthiness in the relevant domain (e.g., practical survival matters may favour intuition; philosophical theorizing may favour reason). Avoid treating the two as wholly opposed; see intuition as often the source of beliefs that reason must harmonise or test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test beliefs by mutual compatibility (reason as harmoniser)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reason is a harmonising, controlling force rather than a creative one... the confirmation, where it is possible, consists, in the last analysis, of agreement with other beliefs no less instinctive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reason to check beliefs for internal consistency and for compatibility with other well-grounded beliefs. When two instinctive convictions conflict, investigate sources of error and prefer the mediated, harmonised position. Treat reason as corrective to blind reliance on single instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware motivated/mood-driven logic
rubrics_metrics.description: When an emotional mood produces a belief, the mind tends to be "very hospitable to any ground that suggests itself," seeking logic to justify an already existing conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and correct for motivated reasoning: if a belief pre-exists emotionally, scrutinize purported logical 'proofs' offered to support it. Avoid constructing or accepting arguments solely because they reach a desired mystical paradox or conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of epistemic method to domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuition and instinct excel in practical, survival‑related matters (e.g., judging friendship), whereas philosophy — dealing with strange, remote objects of thought — demands intellect and patient analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which mode (intuition vs intellect) is epistemically suitable: use intuition for quick practical judgments, but privilege measured intellectual methods for abstract philosophical/metaphysical claims. Do not generalize the success of intuition in one domain to its reliability in all domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of intuition's subjective certainty and fallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "Intuition has a convincingness which is lacking to intellect: while it is present, it is almost impossible to doubt its truth... if it should appear, on examination, to be at least as fallible as intellect, its greater subjective certainty becomes a demerit..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the felt certainty of an intuition as potential evidence of error (it can make deception more irresistible). Require external checks rather than accepting phenomenological certainty as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystical claims about Unity (monism) require scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Mysticism commonly asserts "belief in unity, and its refusal to admit opposition or division anywhere" — e.g., 'good and ill are one' or the Parmenidean claim that reality is one and indivisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of universal unity for logical and empirical coherence. Examine whether asserted paradoxes (identity of opposites) are genuine discoveries or rhetorical outcomes of the mystical mood. Prefer explanations that do not arbitrarily dissolve well‑established distinctions without argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine claims that plurality and division are illusory
rubrics_metrics.description: Question II posed: "Is all plurality and division illusory?" — i.e., the mystical denial of real multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require argument and evidence before rejecting plurality. Test whether the denial of division leads to contradictions (e.g., undermining the very possibility of thought or language) and whether the supposed illusion account explains observable differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize denial of the reality of Time
rubrics_metrics.description: A "third mark" of mysticism is "the denial of the reality of Time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims that past and future are illusory against their implications for causation, memory, change, and linguistic reference. Demand philosophical and/or scientific argumentation for treating temporal distinctions as merely apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate ontological claims about good and evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Question IV posed: "What kind of reality belongs to good and evil?" Mysticism often holds that evil is merely appearance, an illusion produced by analytic division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze ethical claims for their metaphysical status: does the mystical posture imply that cruelty and suffering are unreal? If so, examine the moral and practical consequences (e.g., absence of protest, acceptance) and whether such conclusions are defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish attitude from metaphysical creed
rubrics_metrics.description: Russell's distinction: "If this is the truth, mysticism is to be commended as an attitude towards life, not as a creed about the world... The metaphysical creed... is a mistaken outcome of the emotion, although this emotion... is the inspirer of whatever is best in Man."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value mystical reverence and emotional attitude (humility, reverence, largeness of contemplation) while rejecting untested metaphysical claims derived from that emotion. Treat mystical feelings as aesthetic or ethical dispositions rather than as evidence for metaphysical doctrines unless supported by reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical desires must not dictate truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "The man of science... must lay [ethical hopes] aside while he studies nature; and the philosopher, if he is to achieve truth, must do the same. Ethical considerations... should appear as determining our feeling towards the truth, and our manner of ordering our lives in view of the truth, but not as themselves dictating what the truth is to be."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that moral preferences or hopes do not shape what conclusions are accepted as true. Guard against letting the 'legislative function' of the good determine metaphysical or scientific claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirically inspired scientific temper when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Russell praises the 'impartial temper' that values mean or lowly things and regards observation; he illustrates how scientific observation informed Heraclitus's ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where claims touch on observable matters, demand empirical grounding or at least sensitivity to observational data. Combine reverence or imaginative insight with a scientific impartiality to avoid speculative excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware overreach of mystical logic (paradox as symptom, not proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystical systems often produce paradoxes (e.g., identity of opposites) because "the paradoxes apparently proved by his logic are really the paradoxes of mysticism, and are the goal which he feels his logic must reach."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat paradoxical conclusions with suspicion as they may reflect prior emotional commitments rather than sound inference. Demand rigorous logical scrutiny of steps that produce contradictions or counterintuitive identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize practical reliability as a test of faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where instinct and reason do sometimes conflict is in regard to single beliefs, held instinctively... Where instinct is least liable to error is in practical matters as to which right judgment is a help to survival."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical success (survival, reliable action) as one axis to evaluate the reliability of faculties like instinct/intuition. But do not generalize from practical reliability to domains where different epistemic standards apply (e.g., abstract philosophical inquiry).
